en: Forgive me, O forgive, I bow, I bow; remembering you, O Incomparable,
my heart brims over and rings with the rapture of dance.
With the yearning cry of all my body, in praise of you beyond all mantras,
rhythm descends to right and left into a new birth.
Today my worship dwells in gesture and in song.
What supreme pain makes my soul tremble — the trembling strikes my breast.
Waves play across the sea of peace, and beauty wakes upon it.
All my consciousness, all my sorrow — what worship have they wrought —
may my striving at your feet not die of shame.
Today my worship dwells in gesture and in song.
I have plucked no flower from the grove; no fruit was granted me.
My pitcher is as empty; I have not filled it with holy water.
Through every limb of my body the unbound heart pours an unseizable stream —
let it be spent at your feet in the holy work of worship.
Today my worship dwells in gesture and in song.
To the beat of the dance, Nataraja, undo, undo, undo every bond.
Break the slumber, wake in the heart the rhythm of unfettered song.
At the wind-touch of your feet, on Saraswati's lake of the mind,
age after age, time after time, tune upon tune, beat upon beat,
raise the waves, wake it to rapture with the scent of the stainless lotus.
I bow, I bow, I bow —
may your dance's boundless treasure fill this heart of mine.
In your dance is the form of freedom, in your dance your maya;
in the body of the world, atom by atom, trembles the shadow of the dance.
The swaying, swaying of your world-dance fastens bonds and looses bonds,
age after age, time after time, tune upon tune, beat upon beat,
who can find its end — the thought bewilders the mind.
I bow, I bow, I bow —
may your dance's boundless treasure fill this heart of mine.
Under the dance's sway the rebel atom turned beautiful;
round your two feet moon and sun rang out as anklets of light.
In the life-pang of your dance the numbed world wakes to consciousness,
age after age, time after time, tune upon tune, beat upon beat,
in joy and sorrow your supreme bliss surges into waves.
I bow, I bow, I bow —
may your dance's boundless treasure fill this heart of mine.
In my world your tandava rages, your matted locks atremble.
From world to world I have wandered in the whirling beat of your dance.
O ascetic, O beautiful one, O Shankara, O terrible one,
age after age, time after time, tune upon tune, beat upon beat,
sound the damaru of the dance of life and death, deep as thunderclouds.
I bow, I bow, I bow —
may your dance's boundless treasure fill this heart of mine.
No fear, no fear, none at all.
Let fear lie, let it lie outside.
Wake, conqueror of death, in the heart's surging dance.
O mind, your bonds are broken —
clap your hands — tai, tai, tai!
When you danced the dance of doom, lost to yourself,
O Nataraja, the knot of your matted hair fell loose.
So the Ganges in her freed torrent, mad, loses her way;
her hosts of waves rose swaying in song.
The sun's light answered from across the sky,
sounding words of fearlessness to the homeless one.
Drunk on her own current, she became her own companion;
she who lost all found all along her banks.
In two hands —
Time's cymbals ring forever, right and left, in two hands;
sleep is scattered, dance springs up at each ever-new clash.
They ring in the flower, ring in the thorn, in the ebb and flow of light and shade;
there they ring within the heart, in sorrow, joy and dread.
Beat by beat, at dusk and dawn, waves stir the sea of forms;
in the strife of white and black that rhythm wakes many colors.
Set your song to this beat — practise the tune of tears and laughter;
listen, death and life have called you with the drum of the dance-hall.
In my heart, in ceaseless dance, who is it that dances —
tata thoi-thoi, tata thoi-thoi, tata thoi-thoi.
And with him what a drum forever sounds —
tata thoi-thoi, tata thoi-thoi, tata thoi-thoi.
Laughter and tears, diamond and emerald, swing on his brow;
good and evil tremble in rhythm, beat by beat;
birth dances, death dances, close behind —
tata thoi-thoi, tata thoi-thoi, tata thoi-thoi.
What joy, what joy, what joy —
day and night freedom dances, bondage dances —
on that wave I race in glee, close behind —
tata thoi-thoi, tata thoi-thoi, tata thoi-thoi.
My head is spinning — tadhin tadhin.
Dancing, dancing behind you, my head is spinning — tadhin tadhin.
My feet move to your beat; I cannot hear who says what —
tadhin tadhin.
At your song, whatever madman was in my soul has awakened —
tadhin tadhin.
My bonds of shame, bonds of dress, worship and rites have all slipped away —
tadhin tadhin.
Swung by the wild rush of the dance, every worry has fled —
tadhin tadhin.
Bees of the lotus grove, come to the lotus dwelling.
What nectar-fragrance has come today on the new spring wind.
Round the stainless feet a hundred hundred-petalled lotuses bloomed in rapture;
the news of it sped through heaven and earth, from world to world.
In planets and stars, ray upon ray, a melody rings out;
humming of song, warbling of birds, rise yearning in the ear.
The sea sings its ballad of surges, the wind blows the conch —
the Sama chant rises in the forest leaves, the song of blessing in life.
Come, O new life.
Come, harsh, pitiless, silent one; come, terrible and beautiful.
Come, unloved, joyless, bitter one; come, drenched in tears;
come, unadorned and bare; come, purifier of the heart.
Away with lute and flute, jasmine garlands, full-moon nights, mists of illusion —
come, fierce flame of the sacrificial fire, drinker of the heart's blood.
Come, abode of utmost sorrow; destroy the sprouting seed of hope —
come, battle; come, great victory; come, consummation in death.
A sweet, sweet sound is ringing
in the lotus grove of the heart.
She who dwells in seclusion, lute in hand — the Word in her deathless form —
a vision of golden radiance — where in the soul does she dwell?
The honeyed season wakes day and night; the koel calls in every quarter.
The bee of the mind swoons at her feet in the fragrance.
Come, goddess, come into this light; let me see you once with my eyes —
do not stay hidden in the mind's realm, robed in shadow and illusion.
Rise, sad-faced one; come, it is time.
Come, thirsting heart; put away your wailing.
See, the day is done; the fair has broken, broken up —
all have left the game, each to their own home.
O beggar, to whom are you singing your tune —
the night has fallen dark, the road is very far.
For a soul hungry and thirsting, song has no more use —
now the sitar plays its tune out of key.
So what if I never cross to the far shore.
The wind that would have sped the boat — I let that wind play on my body.
If the voyage never came together, there is still the landing where I can sit.
If my boat of hope has sunk, I shall watch you row your boats.
What lies at hand, what lies in my lap — that is plenty.
Is this to be my whole day's work — gazing weeping toward the far side?
Whatever little I lack here, I will fill it up with my soul.
My wishing-vine grows just there, where my claims lie.
When my footprints fall no more upon this path,
when I row my ferry-boat no more at this landing,
when I have wound up all my buying and selling,
settled, oh settled all my dues and debts,
and my comings and goings cease in this market —
then you need not remember me,
need not gaze at the stars and call me.
When dust gathers on the tanpura's strings,
when thorn-vines climb the doors of the house — ah,
when the flower garden dons thick grass, the dress of exile,
and moss comes creeping round the edges of the pond —
then you need not remember me,
need not gaze at the stars and call me.
Then the flute will play on just so in this playhouse,
the days will pass, will pass,
the days will pass just as the days pass now — ah,
at landing after landing the ferry-boats will fill just as today —
cattle will graze, cowherds will play in that field.
then you need not remember me,
need not gaze at the stars and call me.
Then who says I shall not be there that morning?
This very I will play in every game — ah,
you will call me by a new name, bind me in new encircling arms;
I shall come and go, that same I of all time.
then you need not remember me,
need not gaze at the stars and call me.
That red-earth road beyond the village beguiles my mind.
Oh, toward whom does my mind stretch its hands and tumble in the dust?
It draws me out of the house, clinging to my feet at every step —
it snatches me and carries me off, off to who knows where.
What treasure will it show at which bend, in what strait will it land me —
where at last it ends, thought cannot fathom.
This is what I loved — the dance of light on leaf after leaf.
The mad wind in the sal forest — this is what intoxicates my mind.
Along the red-earth road the market travelers hurry on;
a little girl sits in the dust, arranging her tray of playthings alone —
whatever I see looking before me sets a lute playing in my eyes.
Mine is a bamboo flute; my discipline is the tune of the fields.
My mind is bound by the bond of this earth's soil.
Those who have newly drunk the stream of light from the blue sky —
I have filled my two eyes with the gaze of those children —
I have tuned my lute to the tune of their tender voices.
When the fancy takes me to go far, everyone crowds round and stops me —
the village sky calls me with the beckoning of drumstick blossoms.
The nectar of the near, brother, is not spent, so I feel no hunger for the far —
these little everyday things — I have found no shore or limit to them.
My round of songs for trifling days is not finished even now.
It pleased me, it charmed my mind — that is all I go about singing —
where is the time, day or night? So I dodge all talk of work.
My mind is rapt, my eyes are rapt — it is useless to keep calling me —
they have many hopes; let them heap up much —
I only go about singing; I do not wish to grow any greater.
Dye me in color as you go — go, go now, before your going —
in your own hue, in your secret hue,
in the dawn hue of your young laughter,
in the sorrowful hue of tears.
May the color touch my inmost core, touch all my work,
touch the tip of the evening lamp, touch the deep night's waking.
Before you go, oh wake me as you leave,
setting the sway of your feet astir in my blood.
As stars wake in the breast of the dark night,
as a spring-stream wakes in the chamber of the stony cave,
as thunder wakes in the heart of the cloud,
as rhythm wakes at the center of the world-dance,
so give me a swing as you go, speeding me on the parting road,
putting the bonds of weeping to flight.
My blind lamp gazes toward the void;
it confesses its shame to the stars of the wasted night.
Let the writing fall upon its brow —
your inscription, O flame —
paint on it the mark of victory: this is all it begs.
Alas, on whose road have you set out, forlorn one?
Make me your debtor with the debt of your light.
Your night and my night
are threaded on one strand of light —
alas, lest such fortune slip from me.
Why my mind is beguiled, my mind does not know.
Who is there to forbid it? My mind will not obey.
No one understands it, and it does not understand itself.
Everyone comes to shame it; it simply takes no heed.
Its ferry has crossed to the far side; it stayed on the river's bank.
Their work all done, look, others have gone ahead;
the absent mind does not cast a glance that way.
Who has called me toward the inner world —
oh, they know how to call.
As in Ashwin the shiuli bough
calls the honeybee
at dawn with its song of fragrance.
The homeless one has found a home today, and stays absorbed in its own mind.
Somehow, on wind after wind, the news of it has reached
the ear of that homeless cloud.
The dust of the market is past bearing; it leaves my soul distressed.
Bathe me in the stream of your heavenly river of song.
Let its drum-roll awaken, let it raise a surge of waves in my blood,
let it wash from my limbs every dishonor —
let its murmuring music drown all the clamor.
O beautiful one, with your flowers I once wove a garland —
remind me of that today; make me forget every burning pain.
Call me again, invite me into the lotus grove of your song —
let me drink once more its hidden drops of nectar,
grant me the tilak-mark of its pollen.
I walk alone through this world;
who will tell me the way?
No fear, no fear —
go as your own heart leads,
as the lone bee goes darting on
by the flowers' fragrance alone.
I have heard the call from beyond dream, and so, awake, I wonder —
does anyone ever find the key to the dream-world?
Not to go there, not to gain anything —
it makes no claim at all —
lost from the world is the key to the dream-world.
Within the breast of wanting and getting blooms the flower of the unattained,
and the sky fills with its bewildered fragrance.
The one I go seeking in song — into the soul's deep abyss
whoever has gone down,
that one has stolen away the key to the dream-world.
Absorbed in myself, in a hidden corner, in my workshop of scribbling,
door barred, I carve words and fashion my toys.
In this world's mornings and evenings I am on holiday from every task;
matching word with word, they come to suit color upon color.
Who is there in the world, an eternal child in joy,
who calls me to the world-game, to furnish the playhouse?
On the forest wind at morning he floats his raft of song;
it is he who sets the tremor of tune trembling on the blue wings of bees.
My morning bud falls apart by afternoon;
alas, in between I never saw it when it opened.
Gather up from the dust the petals of the fallen flower;
when there was time, it played me false —
now, at day's end, bring in gleanings, the torn remnant out of season.
The sliver of moon in the dark fortnight gives the darkness solace —
with that let my hope be content — the dream has fled.
You are mad — then with full voice
dare to proclaim it.
If they come rattling at your door,
you stay in your corner and give no answer —
let them all say 'misfit', let them all say 'what use are you'.
Say, 'I am no one at all,
nothing whatever, whatever I may be.'
Hearing it, laughter will rise in the woods,
flutes will sound in every quarter —
the wind will say 'I love you', the sky will bind you with unseen cords.
